title: Dama Defense Strategy: How to Protect Your Pieces
description: Master dama defense strategy: keep pieces paired, shield with the back row, know when to retreat, and trade wisely to avoid losing material to forced captures.
body:
Attack gets the glory in Filipino Dama, but a solid dama defense strategy is what keeps you in games long enough to win them. Because captures are mandatory and you must always take the longest capture chain available, a single unguarded piece can trigger a cascade that costs you three or four pieces in one move. Prevention is far cheaper than recovery.

Defensive play in Dama is not about sitting still and waiting — it is about structuring your pieces so that your opponent cannot find an entry point. A well-defended position limits your opponent's options, forces them to make commitments they do not want to make, and creates the conditions for a counter-attack on your own terms. This article covers the core principles that keep your pieces safe from the opening moves through to the endgame.

Keep Your Pieces Paired: The Core Dama Defense Strategy

The simplest defensive principle in Dama is also the most powerful: never leave a piece without a partner that can cover it. A piece is "covered" when an adjacent friendly piece sits behind it on the diagonal, ready to recapture if the first piece is taken. An opponent who captures a covered piece immediately gives you a free recapture — that is often a trade they will want to avoid.

Pairs do not have to sit side by side on adjacent squares. They just need to be close enough that the rear piece can step in. Think of your pieces in defensive clusters rather than long, strung-out lines. Isolated pieces at the front of a column, with no friendly piece behind them, are the easiest targets on the board.

Spotting Isolated Pieces

Before advancing any piece, ask one question: if my opponent captures this piece, can I recapture immediately? If the answer is no, either bring another piece up to cover it first, or do not advance at all. Advancing without coverage is the most common defensive error beginners make.

  • A piece with no friendly piece on any adjacent diagonal behind it is isolated.
  • A piece sitting on the edge of the board (the side files) has fewer escape diagonals and is harder to cover.
  • Two pieces advancing in parallel, one square apart on adjacent diagonals, provide mutual cover and are much harder to attack than the same two pieces in a single-file column.

Use the Back Row as a Shield

The back row — the row of squares closest to your own side — has a special property: any piece sitting in it cannot be captured from behind, because there is no square behind it. More importantly, a pawn sitting in your back row blocks your opponent from promoting any piece that reaches that row. As long as at least one of your pieces occupies your own back row, your opponent cannot create a flying king there.

The back-row anchor: Keeping one or two pieces in your back row is a classic defensive move. It denies your opponent promotion squares and gives you a solid base to fall back on. Do not empty your back row unless you have a very compelling reason to advance those pieces.

This does not mean parking all your pieces at home — that would simply hand the board to your opponent. It means leaving a rear guard. One piece per corner of your back row is often enough to keep the promotion threat under control while you develop the rest of your position.

Recognizing Dangerous Positions Before They Become Captures

The mandatory-maximum-capture rule means that your opponent is always looking for a position where they can sacrifice one piece to trigger a long chain. A dangerous position usually has these warning signs:

  • A gap between two of your pieces on the same diagonal, with an opponent's piece positioned to jump the first and continue to the second.
  • Your pieces forming a diagonal line of three or more with alternating empty squares — a classic setup for a multi-jump.
  • An opponent's piece on the edge of a cluster you thought was safely grouped, able to enter from an angle you did not check.

Train yourself to count your opponent's available captures before you move. If they currently have no forced capture and your proposed move creates one, reconsider. You want to move in ways that keep your opponent's capture options at zero, or at most limited to single jumps that you can immediately recapture.

When to Retreat vs. When to Hold

Retreating a pawn in Dama is not a sign of weakness — it is a tool. Pawns can only move forward normally, so "retreating" means stepping to a diagonal square that is still forward but out of the threatened line. This is a form of redirection rather than true retreat.

The decision framework is simple:

  • Hold if your piece is covered and retreating would open a worse gap elsewhere in your formation.
  • Redirect if the piece is isolated and a lateral step removes the immediate threat without exposing another piece.
  • Sacrifice deliberately only if you can recapture at least as many pieces back, or if the recapture gives you a king.

Forcing yourself to retreat repeatedly without a plan means your formation is collapsing. If you find yourself retreating three moves in a row, stop and look for the root cause — almost always it is an isolated piece or a gap in your back-row coverage that your opponent has been exploiting.

Trading Pieces to Relieve Pressure

Sometimes the most effective defense is to simplify the position by trading off pieces. If your opponent has built up a threatening cluster on one side of the board, look for an equal exchange that reduces the number of pieces in that area. Fewer pieces means fewer possible capture chains.

A fair trade — one of your pawns for one of theirs — is almost always acceptable when you are under pressure, as long as neither piece being traded is a king. Trading away a king to eliminate a pawn is a poor deal; trading a pawn for a pawn to break up a dangerous formation is often the right call.

Trade to gain, not just to escape: The best trades leave you with better piece placement after the exchange. Before initiating a trade, check where your remaining pieces will sit. A trade that leaves your pieces more cohesive and your opponent's more scattered is a defensive win even if the material count stays equal.

Protecting Your Pieces in the Endgame

As pieces come off the board, open diagonals multiply and flying kings become extremely dangerous. A single opponent king can cover the entire board in one move, so endgame defense shifts heavily toward controlling the key diagonals that a king would use.

If you still have pawns and your opponent has promoted a king, try to keep your pawns in groups of two on the same diagonal so that the king cannot jump one without the other covering the landing square. A lone pawn chased by a flying king across an empty board rarely survives, but two pawns working together can often force a stalemate or buy time to promote one of your own.

The Core Defensive Habit

Every defensive principle in this article comes back to one habit: look at your own position from your opponent's point of view before each move. Ask what captures they can make right now, and what captures your proposed move would create. If the answer gets worse after your move, find a different move. Build this check into your routine and the common defensive errors — isolated pieces, exposed gaps, unguarded advances — will start to disappear from your games naturally.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most important dama defense strategy?

Keep your pieces paired for mutual support. A piece is covered when a friendly piece sits behind it on the diagonal, ready to recapture. Before advancing any piece, ask whether you could recapture immediately if it were taken — if not, bring up cover first or do not advance.

How do I stop my opponent from making long capture chains?

Avoid leaving gaps between your pieces on the same diagonal and do not string your pieces into long single-file columns, which set up multi-jumps. Count your opponent's available captures before every move; if your move would create a forced capture for them, reconsider it.

Why should I keep a piece on my back row?

A pawn on your own back row cannot be captured from behind and, more importantly, blocks your opponent from promoting any piece that reaches that row. Leaving one or two pieces as a rear guard denies promotion squares and gives you a solid base to fall back on.

title: How Many Pieces in Dama? The Starting Count Explained
description: Wondering how many pieces in dama? Each player starts with 12 pieces on an 8×8 board. Learn the setup, the rules for pawns and kings, and the full count.
body:
If you are new to the game, one of the first things you want to confirm is exactly how many pieces in dama each player gets. The answer is straightforward: each player begins with 12 pieces, placing them on the dark squares of a standard 8×8 board. That gives you 24 pieces on the board at the start of every game.

Those 24 pieces — 12 per side — sit on opposite ends of the board, ready to advance toward each other. Understanding why there are 12, where they go, and what happens to them as the game progresses is essential before you make your first move. This article walks through the full setup so you can start a game with confidence.

How Many Pieces in Dama: The Board and the Dark Squares

Filipino Dama is played on an 8×8 board — 64 squares in total. But pieces only ever occupy the dark squares. On an 8×8 grid there are exactly 32 dark squares, and at the start of a game only 24 of them are used: 12 for one player's pieces and 12 for the other's.

Because play happens on dark squares only, each row of eight squares effectively provides only four usable positions. Three rows of four positions gives you exactly 12 pieces per side — that is why the starting count is what it is. It is not an arbitrary number; it follows directly from the geometry of the board.

Where Exactly Do the Pieces Go?

Each player fills the three rows of dark squares closest to their own side of the board. With four dark squares per row and three rows available, that is 4 × 3 = 12 pieces. The two center rows of the board stay empty at the start, forming a gap where the two armies will eventually clash.

A correct starting position looks like this:

  • Rows 1–3 (from one player's perspective): filled with that player's 12 pieces on all available dark squares.
  • Rows 4–5: completely empty — this is the neutral zone.
  • Rows 6–8: filled with the opponent's 12 pieces on all available dark squares.
Quick setup check: Once you have placed all pieces, count the empty dark squares in the center. There should be exactly 8 empty dark squares (two rows of four). If you see more or fewer, something is misplaced.

What the Pieces Look Like

In a physical Dama set, each player's pieces are a distinct color — traditionally one side uses light-colored discs and the other uses dark-colored discs, though regional sets vary. The discs are flat and round, similar to checkers pieces. At the start of the game every piece is a pawn — a plain, single disc with no special marking.

The feel of the game is deliberately simple at the outset: two equal armies of identical pieces facing each other. That equality is what makes the opening decisions interesting. Every choice about which piece to advance and in which direction matters, because all 12 of your pieces have the same value at the start.

Pawns vs. Kings: What Changes During the Game

The Pawn

A pawn is the standard piece. It moves one step diagonally forward on each turn — it cannot step backward during normal movement. When a pawn lands adjacent to an enemy piece and the square beyond that piece is empty, the pawn can (and usually must) jump over it to capture it. The captured piece is removed from the board.

The King

When one of your pawns reaches the far back row — the row that was your opponent's home row at the start — it is promoted to a king, also called a dama. In Filipino Dama, kings are "flying kings": they can slide any number of squares diagonally in any direction, not just one step. A king can also capture backwards, giving it far greater range than a pawn.

Promotion is marked by stacking a second disc on top of the first, creating a taller crowned piece that is visually distinct from a pawn. In digital versions of the game, a crown symbol typically appears on promoted pieces.

Why kings matter for piece count: A king is still just one piece — it does not split or multiply. But because it can cover the whole board in a single move, one king can often outmaneuver several pawns. Losing your last king can end a game very quickly.

What Happens to Captured Pieces

Captured pieces are permanently removed from the board. This is the primary way the piece count shrinks during a game. Filipino Dama enforces mandatory capture: if you have a capture available on your turn, you must take it. Furthermore, if multiple capture lines are possible, you must choose the one that captures the most pieces in a single chain of jumps.

This mandatory-maximum-capture rule means the piece counts on both sides can drop very quickly once captures start. A well-timed chain can remove three or four enemy pieces in one turn, swinging the game dramatically.

How Does This Compare to Checkers?

International draughts (checkers in many countries) also uses an 8×8 board and starts with 12 pieces per side — exactly the same starting count as Filipino Dama. The similarity is not a coincidence; both games descend from the same family of diagonal board games.

The key differences lie in the rules rather than the piece count:

  • Filipino Dama kings fly any number of squares; standard checkers kings move only one step.
  • The mandatory-maximum-capture rule in Dama is stricter — in some checkers variants you may choose which capture to take even if it is not the longest.
  • Win condition in Dama is capturing or completely trapping all enemy pieces; in some checkers variants a draw can be agreed.

So if you already play checkers, the starting setup of 12 pieces per side will feel completely familiar. The differences reveal themselves in how the pieces move once the game gets going.

Summary

Filipino Dama starts with 12 pieces per player on a standard 8×8 board, for a total of 24 pieces. They occupy the three closest rows of dark squares on each player's side, leaving two center rows empty. Every piece begins as a pawn and can be promoted to a flying king upon reaching the opponent's back row. Captured pieces leave the board permanently, and with mandatory-maximum-capture rules in force, games can swing quickly once the action starts.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many pieces does each player have in dama?

Each player starts with 12 pieces. On a standard 8×8 board that is 24 pieces in total at the start of the game, placed on the dark squares of the three rows closest to each player.

How many total pieces are on a dama board at the start?

There are 24 pieces in total at the start — 12 for each player. They occupy 24 of the board's 32 dark squares, leaving 8 empty dark squares across the two center rows.

Why does each player start with exactly 12 pieces?

Pieces only sit on dark squares, so each row of eight provides only four usable positions. Filling the three rows closest to a player gives 4 × 3 = 12 pieces. The count follows directly from the geometry of the 8×8 board.

title: Why Dama Is the Filipino Strategy Board Game
description: Discover why Dama stands as the definitive filipino strategy board game — its cultural roots, strategic depth, and why it has endured for centuries.
body:
Every culture has a game that carries its identity — a pastime woven into the rhythm of daily life, played in kitchens, schoolyards, and town plazas across generations. For Filipinos, that game is Dama. More than mere entertainment, Dama is a filipino strategy board game in the truest sense: a test of foresight, patience, and tactical intelligence played on a humble 8×8 board with twelve pieces per side.

What makes Dama endure while countless other pastimes have faded? The answer lies in a combination of accessible rules, genuine strategic depth, and the way the game mirrors values that run deep in Filipino culture — respect for the opponent, the importance of long-term thinking, and the quiet satisfaction of a well-executed plan. This article explores each of those dimensions and explains why Dama remains relevant and beloved today.

Roots That Run Centuries Deep

Dama belongs to the broad family of draughts games that spread across the world from the ancient Mediterranean, but the version played in the Philippines developed its own distinct character over centuries of local tradition. Filipino communities shaped the rules to fit their own sensibilities — most notably the "flying king," a piece that, once promoted, can slide any distance along a diagonal in a single move rather than stepping just one square at a time.

This rule transforms the promoted piece into a genuine power unit, making promotion a major strategic goal and adding a layer of complexity absent from many Western draughts variants. The flying king is not just a stronger piece; it changes the geometry of the entire board, creating long diagonal threats that demand entirely different defensive responses.

The game was passed down not through written manuals but through play — grandparents teaching grandchildren, neighbors challenging neighbors. That oral, communal transmission is itself part of what makes Dama a cultural artifact. The rules lived in the hands and memories of ordinary Filipinos long before they were formalized.

Simple to Learn, a Lifetime to Master

The Rules in Brief

Learning Dama takes minutes. Each player starts with 12 pieces arranged on the dark squares of the first three rows on their side of the board. Pawns move one step diagonally forward. When a pawn can jump over an adjacent enemy piece into the empty square beyond, it must — captures are mandatory. If multiple captures are available, a player must take the line that captures the most pieces. Chains of captures can cross the board in a single turn.

A pawn that reaches the opponent's back row is promoted to a king — the flying piece — which can then slide any number of squares along any open diagonal. The game ends when one player captures or traps all the opponent's pieces.

Why mandatory capture matters strategically: Because you must capture when a jump is available, your opponent can sometimes engineer a sacrifice — offering a piece to force you into a capturing sequence that leaves your own pieces exposed. Seeing these traps before they are set is the skill that defines experienced Dama players.

Where the Depth Lives

The rules are simple, but the strategy is not. Even at the pawn level, every move carries consequences: advancing too eagerly exposes pieces to sacrifice traps; advancing too cautiously allows your opponent to build a dominant position. The balance between aggression and patience is constant.

Once kings enter the game, positional complexity increases dramatically. A flying king controls multiple diagonals simultaneously. Two kings working in coordination can cut the entire board into zones, herding enemy pawns toward corners where they cannot escape. Learning to use the flying king effectively is a study in geometry and timing.

A Game That Teaches Strategic Thinking

Beyond the mechanics, Dama teaches habits of mind that extend far outside the game:

  • Planning ahead. Every move is a commitment. Before you slide a piece, you must ask what your opponent's response will be, and what your response to that response will be. This chain of if-then thinking is the foundation of strategic reasoning in any domain.
  • Reading the whole board. A player who focuses only on the piece they are moving loses sight of threats forming elsewhere. Dama trains the habit of scanning broadly before acting locally.
  • Accepting consequences. There is no taking back moves in Dama. A decision made is a decision lived with. That accountability sharpens attention and builds discipline.
  • Patience under pressure. A losing position requires calm, methodical defense. Panic leads to rushed moves and compound errors. The game rewards composure.

These are not coincidental benefits. They are the reason parents and teachers across the Philippines have long encouraged children to play Dama, recognizing in it a form of mental exercise that is also genuinely fun.

The Most Accessible Filipino Strategy Board Game

One of Dama's great strengths is that it costs almost nothing to play. A board can be drawn on paper. Pieces can be bottle caps, coins, or stones. In a country where access to expensive leisure activities is uneven, Dama has always been democratic — available to anyone, anywhere, regardless of income or background.

That accessibility has preserved the game's community dimension. Dama is rarely played in silence. Spectators watch and comment. Opponents talk between moves. The game creates a social space as much as a competitive one, and that social warmth is part of what has kept it alive across generations and across the diaspora. Filipino communities abroad carry Dama with them as a piece of home.

Dama in the Digital Age

Today, Dama has found a new home online. Players who once needed a neighbor or classmate as an opponent can now find a game any time, against opponents from across the country or around the world. Online Dama preserves the essential game — the same flying king, the same mandatory captures, the same 8×8 board — while extending its reach to a generation that grew up with screens.

Far from diluting the tradition, digital play has introduced Dama to younger Filipinos who might never have encountered it otherwise, and has allowed the overseas Filipino community to play the game they grew up with no matter where they live. The strategy is unchanged; only the medium is new.

Dama endures because it is genuinely great — a game of real depth wrapped in simple rules, carrying centuries of cultural meaning. Whether played on a hand-drawn board in a provincial backyard or on a phone screen halfway across the world, it remains what it has always been: the Filipino game of strategy.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Dama considered the Filipino strategy board game?

Dama is woven into everyday Filipino life — played in kitchens, schoolyards, and town plazas across generations. It combines accessible rules with genuine strategic depth and reflects cultural values like long-term thinking, respect for the opponent, and patience, which is why it has endured for centuries as the country's signature game of strategy.

What makes Filipino Dama different from Western checkers?

The defining difference is the flying king. Once a pawn is promoted, it can slide any distance along a diagonal in a single move rather than stepping one square at a time. This makes promotion a major strategic goal and creates long diagonal threats that demand entirely different defensive thinking than standard checkers.

Do you need an expensive set to play Dama?

No. A board can be drawn on paper and the pieces can be bottle caps, coins, or stones. This accessibility is part of why Dama spread so widely — anyone, anywhere can play, regardless of income, and today it is also playable online.

title: Dama Endgame Strategy: How to Close Out a Win
description: Master dama endgame strategy: convert material leads into wins with king opposition, triangulation, and edge-forcing techniques in Filipino Dama.
body:
You have more pieces. Your opponent is scrambling. Victory feels close — yet somehow the game drags on, slips into repetition, or ends in a draw you never saw coming. This is one of the most frustrating experiences in Filipino Dama, and mastering dama endgame strategy is what separates players who convert advantages from those who let them bleed away.

The endgame in Dama begins the moment one side holds a meaningful material lead — typically a king against lone pawns, or two kings against one. The rules stay exactly the same: pawns still move one step diagonally forward, captures remain mandatory, and a king (a "flying" piece able to slide any distance along any diagonal) remains your most powerful weapon. But the principles that win the endgame are very different from those that win the middlegame.

Dama Endgame Strategy: Why Material Leads Do Not Win Themselves

A common mistake among developing players is assuming that being up a piece automatically ends the game. In Filipino Dama, that assumption is wrong. A lone king chasing a single pawn across an 8×8 board can fail to force a capture if the pawn finds shelter in a corner or keeps evading along the same diagonal. The defending player exploits mandatory-capture rules to steer the game toward repetition.

Understanding this is the first step: a material advantage gives you the tools to win, but you still need a plan to execute it.

The Three Core Endgame Principles

1. Restrict Before You Capture

Do not chase pieces directly. Instead, use your king's long diagonal range to cut off escape squares. Slide your king to a diagonal that blocks the enemy pawn's forward movement, reducing the number of squares it can safely reach. Once a pawn has only one or two squares available, capturing it becomes straightforward.

Think of it as herding, not hunting. Each move should shrink the opponent's space, not simply pursue their piece.

2. Force Pieces to the Edge and Corners

The edge of the board is a trap. A pawn on the edge can only move in one direction diagonally forward and has no lateral escape. A pawn in a corner is almost always doomed — it has at most one square to move to and cannot change its diagonal.

  • Approach from the center to cut off the retreat to the interior.
  • Use two kings in tandem: one to block the edge, one to close in.
  • Anticipate mandatory-capture sequences — sometimes forcing a capture is the fastest path to pushing the enemy piece toward a corner.
Key reminder: Captures in Dama are mandatory, and you must choose the move that captures the most pieces if more than one capture option exists. In the endgame, you can exploit this rule against your opponent — set up positions where every capture option they have leads them further into a losing corner.

3. King Opposition and Triangulation

Opposition — placing your king so that the opponent's king must give way — is a concept borrowed from chess but applies directly here. When two kings face each other along the same diagonal with an odd number of squares between them, the one whose turn it is to move is in opposition and must concede ground.

Triangulation is the technique of wasting a move to shift the opposition to your favor. Because a flying king can slide to many squares in a single move, you can often "triangle" — move away and return in two moves rather than one — to force your opponent into a worse position. This is subtle but decisive when your opponent has limited moves.

King vs. One or Two Pawns: The Core Endgame Strategy

This is the most common winning endgame scenario. Here is the reliable approach:

  1. Identify the pawn's promotion square. Your opponent wants to reach the back row and promote. Deny that path first.
  2. Cut the diagonal. Slide your king to intercept the pawn's most direct route to promotion.
  3. Shepherd toward the edge. Each move, close off one more escape diagonal until the pawn has nowhere safe to go.
  4. Force the capture. Once the pawn is cornered, position your king for a clean jump and take it.

Against two remaining pawns, target the more advanced or more isolated one first. Removing it simplifies the position and avoids scenarios where a mandatory capture forces you into an unfavorable trade.

Avoiding Draws

Draws are the endgame villain. They can occur through repetition (the same board position arising three times) or simply through a stalemate where the losing side cannot be forced to lose a piece. To avoid them:

  • Never repeat the same position twice if you can help it — vary your approach diagonal.
  • Keep your king active. A passive king that only threatens never delivers.
  • When up two kings against one pawn, coordinate both kings on different diagonals to close escape routes simultaneously.
  • If mandatory-capture rules would force you into a losing repetition, look for a setup move that changes the pawn's position before you commit to the capture sequence.

Endgame Pattern: The Double-King Squeeze

When you have two kings against a lone pawn (or lone king), the double-king squeeze is your most reliable winning method. Place one king on a long diagonal that covers the pawn's forward-left escape, and position the second king to cover forward-right. With both diagonals covered, the pawn is trapped.

The pawn's only moves lead it toward one of your kings or into the edge of the board. From there, a forced capture is just a matter of one or two precise moves. Practice this pattern in your games and it will become instinctive.

The endgame rewards patience and precision. A single imprecise move can let a winning position slip. But once you internalize these principles — restrict, corner, coordinate — you will find that converting a material advantage into a victory becomes a repeatable, reliable process.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best dama endgame strategy when I'm ahead in pieces?

Restrict before you capture. Use your king's long diagonal range to cut off the enemy piece's escape squares, herd it toward an edge or corner where it has almost no moves, then force the capture. Chasing pieces directly usually wastes moves and risks a draw by repetition.

Why won't my material lead win the game automatically?

Being up a piece only gives you the tools to win — you still need a plan to execute it. A lone king chasing a single pawn can fail to force a capture if the defender shelters in a corner or keeps evading along the same diagonal, steering the game toward a repetition draw.

How do I win a two-kings-versus-one endgame?

Use the double-king squeeze: position one king to cover the opponent's forward-left escape diagonal and the second to cover forward-right. With both diagonals controlled, the enemy piece is forced toward an edge or into one of your kings, and a mandatory capture follows in a move or two.

title: Dama Notation: How to Read and Record Moves
description: Learn dama notation — how to number the board squares, write down moves, and record games so you can review, share, and study your Filipino Dama play.
body:
Learning dama notation—the shorthand for recording your games—is one of the most effective ways to improve. When you can write down exactly what happened, you can replay the game afterward, spot where the position turned, and show specific moves to other players for analysis. Notation is also how competitive dama players share puzzles, openings, and endgame studies. This guide explains the numbering system used for Filipino Dama on the standard 8x8 board, and walks through how to write every type of move clearly and unambiguously.

Dama Notation: Numbering the Board

Filipino Dama is played exclusively on the dark squares of an 8x8 board. Since only 32 of the 64 squares are ever used, notation systems number only those 32 dark squares rather than using a column-row grid like chess. The most common convention — consistent with standard draughts notation used internationally — numbers the playable squares 1 through 32.

Squares are counted from the top-left of the board as seen from White's side (the player who moves first, sitting at the bottom). The top row of dark squares is numbered 1–4 from left to right, the next row down is 5–8, and so on, ending with squares 29–32 in White's back row. White's pieces start on squares 21–32; Black's pieces start on squares 1–12.

It is worth sketching this grid on paper the first time you use it — after a few games the square numbers become instinctive and you will not need to look them up.

Writing a Simple Move

A non-capturing move is written as the starting square, a hyphen, and the destination square. For example:

  • 21-17 — a piece on square 21 moves to square 17 (a common White opening move toward the center).
  • 9-14 — a Black piece on square 9 advances to square 14.

Move pairs are written on a numbered line: the move number, then White's move, then Black's reply, separated by a space. A full opening exchange looks like: 1. 21-17 9-14.

Writing a Capture

A capture uses an x instead of a hyphen. The notation shows the square the jumping piece starts from and the square it lands on after the jump — the captured piece's square is not written explicitly but is implied by the geometry (it lies between the two noted squares on the diagonal).

  • 17x10 — a piece on 17 jumps the enemy piece between 17 and 10, landing on 10.

For a multi-jump chain, list every square the piece lands on, separated by x:

  • 17x10x3 — the piece lands on 10 mid-chain, then immediately jumps again to 3, capturing two pieces in a single turn.

Because the maximum-capture rule requires you to take the longest available chain, notation makes it easy to verify after the fact that the correct line was played.

Marking Promotions and Kings

When a pawn reaches the back row and is promoted to king, you can append an equals sign and a capital K to the move: 4-1=K or simply note "(K)" after. Some players just circle the square number in their written scoresheet. The important thing is consistency — pick a convention and use it throughout the game record.

King moves are written the same way as pawn moves (hyphen for non-capturing, x for capturing), but you may optionally prefix the starting square with "K" to make the piece type explicit: K1-14. In informal notation this prefix is usually dropped once both players understand which pieces are kings from context.

A Sample Game Fragment

Here is a short opening in standard notation to illustrate the full format:

1. 21-17 10-15   2. 17x10 6x15   3. 22-18 15x22   4. 25x18

Reading this back: White opens by advancing to 17. Black replies to 15. White captures on 10; Black recaptures on 15. White plays to 18; Black takes on 22. White recaptures on 18 — arriving at a symmetrical exchange position after four move pairs.

Practical tip for recording during play: Keep a small notepad beside the board and write each move immediately after you make it — not after your opponent replies. Memory under time pressure is unreliable. If you miss a move, leave a question-mark placeholder and reconstruct it from the position at the end of the game rather than guessing and corrupting the record. A partial game score is still useful for post-game analysis.

Why Bother Recording?

Notation unlocks several things that informal play cannot. You can replay the game to find the exact move where your position went wrong. You can post the game for another player to review. You can build a personal opening repertoire by documenting which lines work for you and which do not. Over time your collection of recorded games becomes a personalized database — far more useful for improvement than general advice alone.

Even if you mostly play online at filipinodama.com/play/, developing the habit of mentally tracking square numbers as you play sharpens your calculation and helps you see the board more precisely. Start by simply narrating moves to yourself as you make them — the notation will become natural within a few sessions.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does dama notation number the board?

Dama notation numbers only the 32 playable dark squares, 1 through 32, counted left to right and top to bottom as seen from White's side. The top row of dark squares is 1–4 and the bottom row is 29–32. White starts on squares 21–32 and Black on 1–12.

How do you write a capture in dama notation?

A capture uses an x instead of a hyphen, listing the start square and the landing square—for example 17x10. The captured piece's square is implied by the geometry. A multi-jump chain lists every landing square, such as 17x10x3.

Why should you record your dama games?

Recording games lets you replay them to find where a position went wrong, share them for review, and build a personal opening repertoire. Over time your recorded games become a personalized database that is far more useful for improvement than general advice.

title: Dama Forced Capture Strategy: Forcing Captures to Your Advantage
description: Learn the dama forced capture strategy: use mandatory jumps to steer your opponent, remove their best pieces, and win material through deliberate sacrifice.
body:
Most beginners learn that mandatory captures are a constraint — a rule that takes the choice out of their hands. Stronger players learn something else: that constraint cuts both ways. Because your opponent must jump whenever a jump is available, you can engineer the position so that their mandatory capture walks directly into your trap. A sound dama forced capture strategy—engineering jumps your opponent cannot refuse—is one of the clearest dividing lines between novice and intermediate play in Filipino Dama.

Why the Mandatory Rule Is a Weapon

In Filipino Dama, if a capture is available you must take it. If multiple capture chains are available, you must take the one that removes the most enemy pieces. You have no choice in the matter. This rigidity is exactly what makes forcing tactics so powerful — your opponent's response is predictable the moment you set one up correctly.

The simplest version: you deliberately walk a piece into capture range. Your opponent takes it. That jump lands their piece on a square where your waiting piece can jump them right back, winning the exchange or continuing a chain that strips two or three pieces in one turn. You sacrificed one to gain two. The key is that they had no way to refuse the first jump.

The Core Dama Forced Capture Strategy: Bait-and-Recapture

Set up a bait-and-recapture like this:

  1. Place a pawn on a square where an enemy pawn can jump it diagonally forward.
  2. Make sure that after the opponent's jump, their capturing piece lands in range of a second piece you control.
  3. When they take the bait — because they must — execute your recapture.

If the geometry works out, you lose one pawn and immediately recover one or two of theirs. Net result: even or ahead on material. The pawn you sacrificed was the price of admission; the piece or pieces you gained on the follow-up capture are the profit.

This pattern becomes more powerful in the midgame when the board is denser and your opponent has fewer safe squares to land on after a jump.

Directing a Chain Capture

The maximum-capture rule opens a subtler forcing idea: you can influence which chain your opponent takes by controlling which pieces are available to capture. If two chain options both take two pieces but one ends with their piece on a terrible square and the other does not, you want them to take the first. You set this up by making sure the other option is blocked or absent, leaving them the "bad" chain as their only maximum-capture path.

Concretely: arrange your pieces so that only one two-jump sequence is available, and make sure that sequence ends with your opponent's piece isolated at your wing, far from the action, where you can take your time mopping up the rest of the board.

Targeting Kings With Forced Lines

Kings are the most powerful pieces in the game — they slide any distance along any diagonal and can capture from afar. Forcing a king into a bad capture sequence is therefore extremely valuable. The trick is that a king will often have many capture options, so you need to close off alternatives before triggering the sequence.

A common pattern: surround a diagonal with your pawns so that the only available jump for the enemy king leads it to a square it cannot safely leave. Once the king is anchored in a corner or edge by your surrounding pieces, it becomes far less effective, and you can promote your own pawns while it sits idle.

The key mindset shift: Stop asking "which of my pieces can I move safely?" and start asking "which square can I put a piece on that forces my opponent into a jump they will regret?" Every sacrifice has a cost, but if the forced response damages their position more than your sacrifice costs, the trade is in your favour. Plan two moves ahead — the bait, and the consequence.

When Not to Force

Forced captures are not always correct. Avoid them when:

  • Your opponent's mandatory response gives them a better capture chain than the one you planned — calculate all their recapture options before committing.
  • The sacrifice weakens a key defensive square that your opponent can exploit afterward.
  • You are winning material and simplification favors you — forcing tactics usually involve risk. A safe, simple exchange often beats a flashy sequence when you are already ahead.

The best way to develop feel for these situations is repetition. Head to filipinodama.com/play/, try setting up forcing sequences deliberately, and watch what breaks. Pattern recognition in dama comes fastest from active experimentation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a forced capture in dama?

A forced capture happens because captures are mandatory in dama: if a jump is available, your opponent must take it, and if several chains exist they must take the one that captures the most pieces. A forced capture strategy deliberately sets up positions where that obligation walks your opponent into a trap.

How does the bait-and-recapture tactic work?

You place a pawn where an enemy piece can jump it, and arrange a second piece so that after the forced jump the enemy lands in your recapture range. They must take the bait, then you recapture—sacrificing one piece to win one or two back.

When should you avoid forcing a capture?

Avoid forcing when the opponent's mandatory response gives them a better capture chain than yours, when the sacrifice weakens a key defensive square, or when you are already ahead and a simple, safe exchange serves you better than a risky sequence.

title: Dama vs International Draughts: Key Rule Differences
description: Dama vs international draughts: compare board size, pawn movement, mandatory captures, and the flying king to see how these two draughts games really differ.
body:
In any dama vs international draughts comparison, the two games look nearly identical at first glance: both are members of the broad draughts family — two players, dark squares, diagonal moves, mandatory captures. But sit down with someone who has only played one and ask them to compete at the other, and the differences surface quickly. The board is a different size, pawns behave differently, and the flying king changes the whole endgame. This comparison walks through every meaningful rule distinction so you know exactly what to expect when you cross from one game to the other.

The Board: 8x8 vs. 10x10

The most visible difference is the board. Filipino Dama is played on a standard 8x8 chess board — the same grid you already know if you play chess. Each player starts with 12 pieces arranged on the three dark-square rows nearest them, leaving two empty rows in the middle.

International Draughts (also called Polish Draughts) uses a 10x10 board, with each player starting 20 pieces on the four dark-square rows closest to them. The larger grid means more pieces in play, longer opening sequences, and a fundamentally different sense of space. There is more room to manoeuvre before contact, and endgames can stretch significantly longer.

For a Filipino Dama player stepping onto a 10x10 board, the extra rows at first feel like open sky — then gradually become a maze of long-range threats.

Pawn Movement: Forward-Only vs. Backwards Captures

This is the sharpest rule gap between the two games. In Filipino Dama, pawns always move forward — one diagonal step toward the opponent's back row. A pawn cannot step backward, and it cannot capture backward. Every piece of positional tension in the opening and midgame is built around this constraint.

In International Draughts, pawns also move forward only when not capturing — but they can capture in both directions, including backward. This backward capture rule opens up a whole class of tactics that simply do not exist in Filipino Dama: a pawn trapped from behind in Dama is a dead weight; in International Draughts it may still swing around and devour an attacker.

The Flying King

Both games promote a pawn to king when it reaches the opponent's back row, and both give kings far more power than pawns. The rules here are nearly identical in spirit — but the distance covered differs in practical terms based on board size.

In Filipino Dama, a king (or "queen") slides any number of squares along a diagonal in any direction, stopping wherever you choose and capturing from afar by jumping over an enemy piece to any empty square beyond it. This is the classic flying king, sometimes called a "long king."

International Draughts uses the same flying king with the same long-range movement. So on this specific point the two games agree — the main difference is that on a 10x10 board those diagonals are simply longer, giving kings even more reach and making king endgames substantially more complex.

Quick-reference summary
Filipino Dama: 8x8 board, 12 pieces per side, pawns move and capture forward only, flying king.
International Draughts: 10x10 board, 20 pieces per side, pawns move forward but capture in both directions, flying king.
Both games: mandatory captures, must take the maximum-capture line, win by eliminating or trapping all enemy pieces.

Mandatory Captures and Maximum-Take Rule

Both games require captures — you must jump an enemy piece if a capture is available. Neither game lets you pass a jump to make a positional move. If multiple captures are available, both games also require you to take the sequence that captures the most pieces. This maximum-take obligation is one of the defining features of the draughts family and it applies in full to both Filipino Dama and International Draughts.

The practical consequence in International Draughts is that calculating maximum-take lines on a crowded 10x10 board can become extremely involved, with multiple kings and pawns all threatening different capture chains simultaneously.

Dama vs International Draughts: Which Should You Learn First?

If you are coming to draughts fresh, Filipino Dama on the 8x8 board is a more approachable starting point. Fewer pieces, a familiar board size, and the clean constraint of forward-only pawn movement make the position clearer for a beginner. The game is deep enough to take years to master — the flying king alone introduces enormous tactical complexity — but the surface rules are easier to hold in your head.

International Draughts rewards players who already understand the basic draughts logic and want a longer, more calculation-heavy game. The backward capture for pawns and the extra 8 pieces per side significantly increase the branching factor of every position.

Either way, the habits you build in one game transfer to the other: positional control, tempo, sacrifice tactics, and king endgame technique all carry across. Players who are serious about either game often study both. You can sharpen your dama skills right now at filipinodama.com/play/ — no download needed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between dama and international draughts?

Filipino Dama is played on an 8x8 board with 12 pieces per side and pawns that move and capture forward only. International Draughts uses a 10x10 board with 20 pieces per side and pawns that can capture both forward and backward. Both games use mandatory maximum captures and a flying king.

Can pawns capture backwards in international draughts?

Yes. In International Draughts a pawn moves forward only but may capture in both directions, including backward. In Filipino Dama, by contrast, pawns capture forward only.

Which is easier to learn, dama or international draughts?

Filipino Dama is generally the more approachable starting point: fewer pieces, a familiar 8x8 board, and forward-only pawn movement make positions clearer for beginners, while International Draughts is a longer, more calculation-heavy game.

title: Dama Flying King Strategy: How to Use the Flying King
description: Master the dama flying king strategy. Learn how to promote, position, and wield the flying king's long-range diagonal power to dominate Filipino Dama matches.
body:
The flying king is the single most powerful piece on the Filipino Dama board. Unlike a pawn, which can only shuffle forward one diagonal square at a time, a king glides across the full length of any diagonal in any direction—and it can capture from a distance too. Players who understand how to create, position, and activate a flying king can turn a losing material position into a decisive win. This guide to dama flying king strategy explains exactly how to do that.

What Makes the Flying King Different

When a pawn reaches your opponent's back row, it is immediately promoted to a king. From that point on, the piece follows entirely different rules. A flying king can move diagonally forward, backward, left-forward, right-forward—any diagonal direction—and for any number of empty squares in a single turn. It is not limited to one step.

Captures also change. A king can jump an enemy piece from any diagonal distance, provided the squares between them are empty, and then land on any empty square along that diagonal beyond the captured piece. This gives the king enormous flexibility: you choose both the angle of attack and the landing square, making it extremely difficult to pin down.

Getting Your First King: Speed vs. Safety

Promotion is not free. Racing a single pawn to the back row is tempting, but an isolated pawn that sprints ahead is easy to intercept and trap. The most reliable path to promotion involves two or three pieces advancing in a loose wedge so that they cover each other. When one piece gets close to the back row, your opponent is forced to respond—either they let it promote, or they sacrifice material to stop it.

Watch for "promotion races" in the mid-game: both players often have a pawn near the back row simultaneously. In those moments, count: if your piece promotes first and immediately captures your opponent's advancing pawn before it promotes, you swing the king advantage to zero and keep the material lead.

Dama Flying King Strategy: Positioning for Maximum Impact

Use Long Diagonals

The king's strength scales with diagonal length. A king sitting near the edge of the board can only threaten one diagonal direction effectively; a king near the center threatens four diagonals at once. After promotion, slide your king toward a central square as soon as it is safe to do so. From there, a single move can reach almost any square on the board.

Attack from Behind

One of the most disruptive things a flying king can do is slide behind your opponent's pawn formation. Because pawns can only move forward, they cannot directly defend against a king attacking from the rear. Pawns in the back rows of your opponent's territory are almost helpless against a king that has slipped behind them—they can't turn around.

Create Threats on Two Diagonals Simultaneously

Position your king so that it threatens two different enemy pieces in the same turn. Your opponent can only block one diagonal per move. If they guard one piece, your king swings to the other. This "fork" tactic is far more achievable with a flying king than with regular pawns, and it is a reliable way to win material exchanges.

Landing square matters most. After a king captures, you choose where along that diagonal it lands. This choice often determines whether the king can chain into a second capture immediately. Before committing, scan the full diagonal for follow-up jumps—sometimes landing one square further out opens a multi-capture chain that removes three or four pieces in a single turn.

Defending Against an Opponent's King

When your opponent has a flying king and you do not, your immediate goal is containment. Group your pawns so they cover each other's diagonals, leaving no long open lanes for the king to slide into. A king surrounded by a tight cluster of pawns loses most of its power—it cannot land safely if every square beyond the cluster is blocked.

Your second priority is to promote your own pawn as quickly as possible. A king-versus-king endgame is a more even contest than king versus pawns. Even if you are down in material, two kings chasing each other can sometimes force a draw if one player cannot maneuver out of a corner.

The King in Chain Captures

Mandatory capture applies to kings just as it does to pawns, and the requirement to maximize captures in a chain applies too. A flying king can extend chains significantly further than a pawn because it can reach pieces across the board in a single jump. When you see a capture chain forming, trace the king's path through all possible routes and pick the one that removes the most pieces—that is the move the rules require, and it is usually the winning one too.

For a primer on promotion itself, see our guide on how a pawn becomes a king. Then head to filipinodama.com/play/ and practice positioning a newly promoted king—the board highlights legal moves, making it easy to see just how far a flying king reaches.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does a flying king move in dama?

A flying king moves diagonally in any direction—forward or backward—for any number of empty squares in a single turn. It can also capture an enemy piece from a distance and land on any empty square along that diagonal beyond the captured piece.

What is the best dama flying king strategy?

Promote safely by advancing pieces in a loose wedge, then slide your king toward a central square so it commands multiple long diagonals. Use it to attack from behind enemy pawns, create two-diagonal forks, and extend the chain captures the rules require you to take.

How do you defend against an opponent's flying king?

Group your pawns so they cover each other's diagonals and leave no long open lanes for the king to slide into, then race to promote your own pawn. A king-versus-king endgame is far more even than king versus a loose cluster of pawns.

title: Can You Move Backwards in Dama?
description: Can you move backwards in dama? Pawns can only move and capture forward, while a king flies any diagonal direction. Here is the full rule, clearly explained.
body:
It's one of the most common questions from players who are just picking up Filipino Dama: can you move backwards in dama? The short answer is "it depends on which piece you're moving." Pawns and kings follow completely different rules in this regard, and understanding the distinction is fundamental to playing the game correctly. Here is the full picture.

Pawns: Forward Only

A regular pawn in Filipino Dama can only move diagonally forward—one step at a time, toward your opponent's side of the board. It cannot move sideways, and it absolutely cannot step backward under normal movement. This is identical to how pieces work in international draughts or standard checkers.

Why this restriction? It forces you to think ahead. Because you cannot simply retreat a pawn that steps into danger, every forward move is a commitment. Players who move pawns carelessly, without considering what the position will look like two turns later, frequently find their pieces stranded in no-man's land with nowhere safe to go.

Can a Pawn Capture Backwards?

This is where Filipino Dama diverges from some regional variants. In Filipino Dama, pawns cannot capture backwards. A pawn's capture must also be forward—jumping over an adjacent enemy piece diagonally into the empty square beyond, and that square must be in the forward direction. If an enemy piece is sitting behind your pawn, you cannot jump it no matter how tempting it looks.

This rule is often confused because some house rules or regional variants do allow backward captures for pawns. If you have played another version before, be aware that the standard Filipino Dama rule is forward-only movement and capture for pawns, full stop.

Kings: Complete Diagonal Freedom

Promotion changes everything. When a pawn reaches your opponent's back row, it is promoted to a king—also called a "flying king" in Filipino Dama. A king is not limited to one square or one direction. It can slide any number of squares diagonally in any direction, including backwards, until it hits the edge of the board or is blocked by another piece.

This flying-king rule is one of the features that sets Filipino Dama apart from American checkers, where a king can only move one square at a time. The dama king is substantially more powerful: it can threaten pieces from across the board, retreat to safety in one move, and execute long-range captures that jump over an enemy piece from any diagonal distance, landing on any available square beyond.

King capture distance. When a king captures, it jumps over the enemy piece and can land on any empty square along that diagonal beyond the captured piece—not just the first one. Choose your landing square carefully; the position you land on determines whether you have follow-up captures available in a chain.

A Quick Reference

  • Pawn moving: Diagonally forward only, one square.
  • Pawn capturing: Diagonally forward only, jumping one enemy piece into an empty square beyond.
  • King moving: Diagonally in any direction, any number of empty squares.
  • King capturing: Diagonally in any direction, jumping one enemy piece from any distance, landing on any empty square beyond it.

Can You Move Backwards in Dama? Strategic Implications

Knowing that your pawns cannot retreat makes formation discipline critical. A lone pawn that has advanced too far ahead of its teammates is exposed—your opponent simply needs to get a piece beside and behind it to cut off any further movement. Advance in groups so that pieces can cover each other's flanks.

The king's backward mobility, on the other hand, means that one promoted piece can completely destabilize your opponent's rear. Many games are decided by which player first promotes a pawn and then uses that king to sweep through the board from behind. Protecting your own back row while racing to create a king is often the central tension of mid-game play. For a deeper dive into the promotion moment itself, read our guide on how a pawn becomes a king.

Ready to test these rules in a live game? Play for free at filipinodama.com/play/ and watch the legal moves highlight on the board—it will make the forward-only pawn rule instantly clear.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you move backwards in dama?

It depends on the piece. A regular pawn can only move diagonally forward, one square at a time, and cannot step or capture backward. A king, or flying king, can move and capture diagonally in any direction—including backwards—across any number of empty squares.

Can a pawn capture backwards in Filipino Dama?

No. In standard Filipino Dama a pawn's capture must be forward only. Some regional or house variants allow backward captures, but the standard rule is forward-only movement and capture for pawns.

How does a king move differently from a pawn?

A king can slide any number of empty squares diagonally in any direction, including backward, and can capture an enemy piece from a distance, landing on any empty square beyond it. A pawn is limited to a single forward diagonal step.

title: Dama Opening Moves: Start Strong
description: Learn the best dama opening moves to control the board from turn one: center control, tempo, and avoiding early blunders in Filipino Dama.
body:
The first few moves of a dama game set the tone for everything that follows. A weak opening leaves gaps in your formation that an experienced opponent will exploit in under ten turns. A strong one gives you active pieces, central squares, and—crucially—options. This guide breaks down the core principles behind good dama opening moves so you can walk into any game with a plan.

Why Openings Matter More Than You Think

In Filipino Dama, pieces move only diagonally forward, and captures are mandatory. That combination means the early game shapes the battlefield fast. Once a sequence of captures begins, you follow its chain to the end—you don't get to stop and reconsider. This is why your setup before the first capture matters enormously: the structure you build in the first four to six turns determines which capture chains are available to you and which ones your opponent can force on you.

Two things you want from an opening: central presence and a solid back row. Pieces near the center of the board have more diagonal lanes to move along, giving you more ways to attack and more ways to retreat. A guarded back row, meanwhile, delays your opponent from promoting a pawn to a flying king—the most powerful piece on the board.

The First Principles of Dama Opening Moves

1. Advance Toward the Center First

On an 8×8 board your 12 pieces start on the three rows nearest you. The four central columns—columns 3 through 6—are the most contested. Move pieces along those lanes before extending to the edges. A piece on a central dark square threatens two diagonals ahead; an edge piece only threatens one. Central pieces also act as natural anchors that support the pieces around them.

2. Do Not Rush a Lone Piece Forward

Sending a single pawn sprinting toward your opponent's back row in the first two turns feels aggressive, but it usually backfires. An isolated lead piece is easy to trap—your opponent can place two pieces so that no matter where it jumps next, a counter-capture is waiting. Advance in coordinated pairs so your pieces protect each other.

3. Maintain a Second Rank Defender

Leaving your own back row completely unoccupied early gives your opponent a runway. Keep at least one or two pieces on your back three rows throughout the opening. These defenders plug lanes and make it much harder for an opponent's piece to slip through and promote.

A Practical Opening Sequence

There is no single "correct" opening in dama the way chess has named openings, but the following approach works well for both beginners and intermediate players:

  1. Turn 1–2: Advance your two innermost center pieces one step forward each. This stakes a claim on the central diagonal lanes immediately.
  2. Turn 3–4: Bring up the pieces directly behind your center pieces to support them. You now have a two-deep central formation—strong enough to resist a single-piece attack.
  3. Turn 5–6: Expand one step to the left or right depending on where your opponent is building pressure. You want a slight diagonal bias toward whichever side looks more open.
The tempo trap. If your opponent moves a piece that puts your piece in a position to capture, check carefully before jumping. Mandatory capture is a rule, but a forced jump can also be a trap—your opponent may have set up a counter-capture that removes two of your pieces for one of theirs. Count the exchange before you leap.

Common Opening Mistakes to Avoid

  • Overloading one side. Stacking all your pieces on the left or right wing leaves the other half of the board empty. A savvy opponent will flood that side and threaten multiple promotion squares at once.
  • Moving the same piece twice in a row. Unless a double jump is on offer, each move should develop a new piece. Repositioning the same pawn twice in the opening wastes tempo while your opponent gains ground.
  • Ignoring back-row protection. It can feel passive, but leaving at least one piece guarding the corners of your back row prevents embarrassing one-move promotions early in the game.

Reading Your Opponent's Opening

Pay attention to which side your opponent is weighting. If all four of their first moves push pieces down the left flank, their right side is soft—probe it gently. If they advance in a balanced line, they're likely playing for a mass exchange in the middle; prepare to win the resulting capture chain by counting pieces before the collision.

Strong dama opening moves are not about memorizing patterns. They are about applying three principles consistently: claim the center, advance in pairs, and keep a defender home. Once those habits are automatic, you'll find yourself in favorable mid-game positions far more often—and favorable positions win games. Get to the board and put it into practice at filipinodama.com/play/.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best dama opening move?

There is no single named best opening in dama, but the strongest dama opening moves advance your two innermost center pieces one step forward to claim the central diagonal lanes. Central pieces threaten two diagonals at once and act as anchors for the pieces around them.

Should I attack early in dama?

No. Sending a lone pawn forward in the first two turns usually backfires, because an isolated piece is easy to trap. Advance in coordinated pairs so your pieces protect each other, and keep one or two defenders on your back rows during the opening.

Why does the opening matter in dama?

Because pawns move only forward and captures are mandatory, the structure you build in the first four to six turns determines which capture chains are available to you and which your opponent can force on you. A weak opening leaves gaps an experienced player exploits quickly.

title: The History of Dama in the Philippines
description: Explore the rich history of dama Philippines — from Spanish colonial origins to a beloved family tradition, and how the game is being revived online today.
body:
Few games are as deeply woven into Filipino daily life as dama. Played on street corners, in barrios, and under the shade of acacia trees, the history of dama in the Philippines spans centuries and touches on colonialism, culture, and the quiet creativity of a people who made a foreign game their own.

This is the story of how a draughts-like game from Europe took root in the Philippines, evolved its own distinct rules, and became a beloved national pastime.

Origins: Draughts Arrives With the Spanish

The word dama comes from Spanish, where it means "lady" or "queen" — the title given to a promoted piece in the Spanish version of draughts. Spain colonised the Philippines for more than three hundred years, from 1565 to 1898, and brought many aspects of Iberian culture with them, including board games.

Spanish draughts, itself descended from a medieval game called alquerque that spread through Europe from the Arab world, made its way to the archipelago during this colonial period. The board, the diagonal movement, and the concept of capturing by jumping over an opponent all trace back to this lineage — a heritage shared with checkers, the Turkish game of dama, and several other regional variants across the globe.

A Filipino Game Emerges

What makes Filipino Dama distinct is the flying king. In international draughts and most checkers variants, a promoted King moves only one or two squares. In the Filipino version, a King becomes a powerful long-range piece that can slide any number of squares diagonally — in any direction — and capture from a distance by jumping over an enemy piece with an empty square beyond it.

This rule amplifies the importance of promotion and gives the game a different strategic character from its European ancestors. Scholars and game historians note that this flying-king rule is common across Southeast Asian draughts variants, suggesting that regional exchange — not just Spanish influence — shaped the game Filipinos play today.

The mandatory capture rule and the requirement to take the maximum number of pieces in a chain are also central to Filipino Dama, forcing active, aggressive play and making defensive stalling far less viable than in, say, American checkers.

Dama as a Cultural Institution

By the twentieth century, dama was deeply embedded in Filipino social life. It required no expensive equipment — a hand-drawn grid on cardboard and bottle caps for pieces were enough. Grandparents taught grandchildren. Neighbours competed in informal tournaments in the plaza. The game was associated with patience, sharpness of mind, and the pleasure of quiet rivalry.

Cultural note: In many Filipino provinces, dama is still played under the term damas, a plural form reflecting its everyday, communal nature — not a competitive sport but a shared pastime.

Schools included dama in their traditional games curricula alongside other Filipino pastimes like sungka, patintero, and tumbang preso. The Department of Education periodically reintroduced these games as part of broader efforts to preserve indigenous and culturally rooted activities for younger generations.

Dama and Damath: A Modern Relative

In 1975, Filipino educator Jesus Huenda invented Damath — a hybrid of dama and mathematics where each square carries a numerical value and capturing pieces involves arithmetic operations. Damath became a fixture in Philippine schools and is still used today as an educational tool. It is sometimes confused with traditional dama, but the two are distinct: Damath is an academic innovation, while Filipino Dama is the centuries-old folk game that inspired it.

The Digital Revival

For much of the late twentieth and early twenty-first century, dama faced the same pressures that traditional games everywhere do: the rise of digital entertainment, mobile phones, and global gaming platforms drew younger Filipinos away from street-corner boards. The game did not disappear — it simply receded from the foreground of popular culture.

The internet changed that dynamic. Online platforms dedicated to Filipino Dama have emerged, allowing Filipinos in Manila, in the provinces, and in the diaspora across the world to play against each other in real time. These platforms carry the exact rules of the traditional game — flying king, mandatory capture, maximum capture chain — ensuring the authentic experience travels with the player wherever they are.

Filipino Dama at filipinodama.com/play/ is part of this revival: a free, browser-based implementation of the game played by generations of Filipinos, now accessible on any device.

Why the History of Dama in the Philippines Still Matters

Dama endures because it rewards the kind of thinking Filipinos value: patience, reading your opponent, and choosing the right moment to act. It is a game that can be learned in minutes and studied for years. Its colonial roots are real, but what Filipino players made of those roots — the flying king, the aggressive capture rules, the communal culture around the board — is entirely their own.

Playing dama today is an act of cultural continuity. Every game connects you to the players who came before, to grandparents on bamboo benches and schoolchildren on tiled floors, all playing on the same eight-by-eight grid with the same diagonal logic that has crossed centuries and oceans.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where did dama originate?

Dama descends from Spanish draughts, which itself grew out of a medieval game called alquerque that reached Europe from the Arab world. Spain introduced it to the Philippines during the colonial period between 1565 and 1898, where it gradually evolved its own distinct rules.

Is dama a Filipino game?

Its roots are colonial, but the version played in the Philippines is distinctly Filipino. The flying king, the mandatory capture rule, and the requirement to take the maximum number of pieces give Filipino Dama a character of its own, shaped by both Spanish influence and wider Southeast Asian draughts traditions.

What is the difference between dama and Damath?

Dama is the centuries-old folk game. Damath, invented by Filipino educator Jesus Huenda in 1975, is a hybrid of dama and mathematics where capturing pieces involves arithmetic. Damath is an educational tool inspired by dama, not the traditional game itself.

title: Common Dama Mistakes to Avoid as a Beginner
description: Avoid the most common dama mistakes to avoid: ignoring mandatory captures, neglecting promotion, trading badly, and forgetting the flying king's range. Fix them fast.
body:
Every dama player starts out making the same errors. The good news is that once you know what to look for, the dama mistakes to avoid are easy to correct. Fixing even two or three of them can immediately bump your win rate and make your games feel far more intentional.

Here are the mistakes that show up most often in beginner play, and what to do instead.

Mistake 1: Ignoring the Mandatory Capture Rule

This one catches new players off-guard constantly. In Filipino Dama, if a capture is available on your turn, you must take it — you cannot choose to move a different piece to a safer square instead. Worse, if multiple capture paths exist, you must take the one that captures the most pieces.

Beginners often miss this entirely and move freely as if dama were checkers with optional captures. The result: illegal moves, arguments, and lost games. Before every turn, scan the entire board for capture opportunities — yours and your opponent's — before deciding anything.

Mistake 2: Rushing Pieces Forward Without a Plan

It feels natural to advance as many pieces as possible as fast as possible. But racing forward with no coordination leaves individual pawns exposed and easy to capture in a chain. Your opponent only needs to set up one forced sequence to clean up three pieces in a single turn.

Move pieces forward in clusters that support each other. Two pieces that protect each other are worth far more than two pieces scattered across the board.

Mistake 3: Neglecting Promotion

Beginners frequently get distracted chasing individual captures and forget to push pawns toward the back row. Promotion to a King is massive — a King slides any distance diagonally in any direction and can capture from afar, making it many times more powerful than a pawn.

Even one King while your opponent has none can be a game-winning advantage. Always keep promotion in mind. If a pawn is one or two squares from the back row, prioritise its advance unless the board forces otherwise.

Mistake 4: Trading Pieces Without Purpose

New players sometimes trade piece for piece reflexively, thinking it is neutral. It rarely is. If you give up a pawn that was close to promotion in exchange for one of your opponent's back-row pawns, you have made a bad trade. Context determines value: a well-positioned pawn is worth more than an isolated one.

Rule of thumb: Before any capture, ask whether the piece you are about to take is actually valuable — and whether the piece you are about to expose is worth losing.

Mistake 5: Forgetting the Flying King's Range

When your opponent promotes a pawn to a King, beginners often underestimate how dangerous it is. A King does not just step one square — it slides the entire diagonal. A pawn sitting three squares away from an enemy King is not safe. It is one move away from being captured.

Once a King is on the board, always trace every diagonal it occupies and treat pieces along those lines as threatened. The same applies to your own King: use that long reach aggressively to threaten multiple pieces at once.

Mistake 6: Playing Too Passively at the Edges

Corner and edge squares feel safe because pieces there cannot be jumped from as many angles. But parking too many pieces at the edges means they are out of the fight, doing nothing while your opponent builds up central control and promotion threats. Passive edge play leads to being outnumbered in the center when it matters most.

Mistake 7: Not Thinking About Trapping

There are two ways to win in Filipino Dama: capture all enemy pieces, or trap your opponent so they have no legal move. Beginners focus entirely on captures and never consider manoeuvring to block. In endgames with just a few pieces each, boxing in the opponent is often faster and more reliable than chasing them across the board.

Start thinking about limiting your opponent's space — not just reducing their piece count.

Fix These Dama Mistakes to Avoid — One at a Time

Do not try to correct everything in a single game. Pick one item from this list — the mandatory capture rule is the best starting point — and focus on it until it becomes automatic. Then move to the next. Within a few sessions you will notice your games becoming tighter, your losses fewer, and your wins more decisive.

The fastest way to learn is repetition. Head to filipinodama.com/play/ and start a game right now with these fixes in mind.

The most common mistake is ignoring the mandatory capture rule — playing as if captures were optional like in some checkers variants. In dama, if a capture is available you must take it, and you must take the path that captures the most pieces. Missing this leads to illegal moves and lost games.

Why do beginners lose so many pieces at once in dama?

Usually because they rush pieces forward without support. A lone advanced pawn is easy to set up for a forced multi-jump that wins two or three pieces in a single turn. Moving pieces in mutually defending clusters prevents this.

Is a pawn far away from an enemy King safe?

No. A flying King slides the entire diagonal, so a pawn three or more squares away on the same open diagonal can be captured in one move. Always trace every diagonal an enemy King occupies and treat pieces on those lines as threatened.
